title: Al-Malik, the King
hook: the King, owner of everything, and so nothing is really yours

segments.voice: Yesterday, rahmah: mercy in a hundred parts, one sent to earth, and mercy that outruns anger. Your line was mercy wins. Did forgiveness get to the starting line first? Day two hundred thirty-eight.

Think of a library book you loved. You carried it everywhere for three weeks. You folded a corner, maybe, and felt bad about it. You read it in bed and on the bus. It felt like yours. And then the due date came, and you took it back, because it never was. In Medina, a woman named Umm Sulaym lost her little son while her husband, Abu Talha, was away. When he came home, she fed him and let him rest. Then, as the report in Sahih Muslim tells it, she asked him a question: if people lent something to a family, and then asked for it back, would the family have the right to refuse? Today: Al-Malik, the King.
screen: `A LIBRARY BOOK, DUE BACK.` → `UMM SULAYM'S QUESTION.` → `CAN YOU REFUSE TO RETURN A LOAN?`

segments.voice: No, said Abu Talha. Then, she said gently, count your son as returned. He was hurt, and he went to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who prayed for blessing on the two of them. The picture behind her question is the name we're learning. Al-Malik comes from the root m-l-k, to own, to possess, to rule. The same root gives malik, king, and mulk, sovereignty, and in the Fatiha there are two accepted readings of one line: Maliki yawm id-din, King of the Day of Judgment, and Maaliki, Owner of it. Both are recited, and both are true. The Qur'an names Him al-Malik in al-Hashr. Here is Pickthall: He is Allah, than whom there is no other God, the Sovereign Lord. And in an-Nas, the King of mankind. Bukhari and Muslim record the Prophet describing the Day when Allah will fold up the heavens and take the earth in His hand, and say: I am the King. Where are the kings of the earth? Every crown and every title, gone quiet. If He is the Owner, then what we call mine is held on loan: the house, the phone, the body, even the children we love. That's not meant to make things cheap. A borrowed thing is treated with care. It's meant to loosen the grip. Muslims say at any loss, in words from al-Baqarah that Pickthall renders: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning. This week began with the beautiful names, the name of names, and mercy vast and near. It ends with the King.
screen: `COUNT YOUR SON AS RETURNED.` · `M-L-K — TO OWN, TO RULE.` · `WHERE ARE THE KINGS OF THE EARTH?` · `WHAT'S MINE IS HELD ON LOAN.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING IS LENT.`

segments.voice: Pick up something small that you think of as yours. Your phone, your keys, a ring, a cup. Hold it in your open hand and look at it. Say quietly: this is lent to me. Notice what happens in your chest. Maybe a little resistance. Maybe some relief. Then set it down gently, and rest your hands on your own knees, and notice that your hands are lent too. If you pray, you can say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. The bell holds the time.
Al-Malik. The King, the Owner of everything, so that all we hold is lent, to be cared for and one day returned. Today's word.

Your line: everything is lent. Today, when you catch yourself gripping something, a possession, a plan, an argument, hold it like a library book: with care, and ready to give back. Day two hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un (we belong to Allah and to Him we return) at news of any loss, from a death to a broken cup, and many speak of wealth, family and life as an amanah, a trust held for a time.

myth: the Fatiha's line about the Day has only one accepted reading
two: Maliki, King, and Maaliki, Owner. both are recited.
Muslims say we are Allah's and to Him we return only at a death
it's said at any loss, great or small.
a hadith pictures Allah asking, where are the kings of the earth?

fork.setup: Umm Sulaym asks her husband: if something lent is asked back, may the family refuse? what does he say?
options: yes, if they've grown to love it
only if they're paid for it
fork.reveal: no. then she told him their son had died: count him as returned. the Prophet prayed for blessing on them (Muslim).

original.note: Arabic: the King, from m-l-k, to own and to rule.

trapdoor: what you thought: God as a king on a throne.
what it means: the Owner of everything, so all we hold is lent: cared for, and returned.
what a scholar hears: m-l-k gives malik, maalik and mulk; the two canonical readings of 1:4; Bukhari 4812 and Muslim 2787, where are the kings of the earth?
